title: London Burns, 1666: Why Did Samuel Pepys Bury His Parmesan Cheese?
description: In the first days of the Great Fire of London in 1666, Samuel Pepys went from going back to sleep and carrying a message to the King, to moving his valuables in his nightgown and putting wine and cheese into a pit in the yard. This episode follows his diary for September 2–6. Where the fire started is something he was told; how heavy the cheese was, what it cost and whether he ever dug it up, these days' entries do not say. The pictures are cartoon illustrations, not images of the actual scene. Information checked on 2026-10-19.

chapters.pf001: Sept 4, evening: Pepys puts his cheese in the second pit
chapters.pf006: Sept 2, before dawn: Pepys sees the fire and goes back to bed
chapters.pf023: Sept 2: Pepys urges the King to pull down houses
chapters.pf040: Sept 2, night: the blaze forces Pepys to pack
chapters.pf052: Sept 3: Pepys sends off his valuables in his nightgown
chapters.pf065: Sept 4: two pits are dug, one after the other
chapters.pf083: Sept 5: the fire reaches the end of Pepys's lane
chapters.pf103: Sept 6: Pepys leads men to a fire and unloads his goods

pf001.text: On September 4, 1666, at dusk, in a London yard, Samuel Pepys was digging the day's second pit with Sir William Penn.

pf002.text: They put their wine in; then he put his Parmesan in too.

pf003.text: How close did the fire come to make him trust the dirt?

pf004.text: Did the fire finally reach his house?

pf005.text: And does his diary say what became of that cheese?

pf006.text: Two days earlier, before dawn on September 2, his maid Jane spotted a fire in the City.

pf007.text: She woke Pepys. In his nightgown, he went to the window.

pf008.text: He thought the fire was behind Mark Lane, still well away from home.

pf009.text: So he really did go back to bed and to sleep.

pf010.text: In the morning he even thought the fire looked smaller. Was the City really safe?

pf011.text: But Jane had news: she'd heard over 300 houses had burned.

pf012.text: Jane only heard it; Pepys had to see for himself.

pf013.text: Up high in the Tower, he at last saw houses by the bridge burning.

pf014.text: The bridge fire made him fear for a friend's house there.

pf015.text: That distant red glow now had streets and families in it. Where would they go?

pf016.text: A Tower official said it began at a King's baker's house in Pudding Lane.

pf017.text: Pepys was told this; he didn't see the fire start.

pf018.text: From a boat, he watched people load their goods onto barges.

pf019.text: On the river, he saw his friend's house had already burned.

pf020.text: Some threw what they couldn't move into the river.

pf021.text: Some stayed until the fire was at their door, then ran to the boats.

pf022.text: The wind drove it into the City. Who could stop it?

pf023.text: Pepys left the river and hurried to Whitehall.

pf024.text: Before the King and the Duke of York, he reported what he'd seen.

pf025.text: Only pulling down houses in its path could stop it, he said.

pf026.text: The King: tell the Lord Mayor not to hesitate.

pf027.text: The Duke of York offered soldiers if needed.

pf028.text: The Lord Mayor looked utterly spent. Could he still lead the demolition?

pf029.text: Pepys noted his complaint: no one obeys, and the fire's too fast.

pf030.text: He'd been up all night, he said, and needed rest.

pf031.text: He said he needed no more soldiers, and walked off.

pf032.text: Even the churches were crammed with people's goods.

pf033.text: People hauled bundles; carts were piled high with goods.

pf034.text: Pepys noted tar in Thames Street, and oil and wine in the warehouses. And what about his own wine?

pf035.text: Yet at noon he went home to his invited guests.

pf036.text: The meal was still lavish, but all minds were on the fire.

pf037.text: At dinner, Mrs Batelier came asking after two relatives; Pepys noted their houses had burned.

pf038.text: After dinner, goods taken in that morning were being moved farther off.

pf039.text: Back on the river: how far had the fire got now?

pf040.text: From the water, the fire had spread farther above and below the bridge.

pf041.text: The river was crowded with boats of goods.

pf042.text: Pepys also saw that many boats even carried a pair of virginals.

pf043.text: Up close, into the wind, flying sparks soon drove him off.

pf044.text: The sparks lit house after house, several doors apart.

pf045.text: At dusk, from the far bank, the fire looked like a long arch.

pf046.text: He wrote that the sight made him weep.

pf047.text: Back home, Tom, whose house had burned, came to stay with what he'd saved.

pf048.text: With news of the fire pouring in, they packed up their own things. Where to move them first?

pf049.text: By moonlight they carried goods into the garden. But would it hold everything?

pf050.text: Tom helped move money and iron chests to the cellar. Pepys hardly slept.

pf051.text: Moving again at dawn, which valuables go first?

pf052.text: Pre-dawn, September 3: a neighbor sent him a cart.

pf053.text: In his nightgown, Pepys rode with the money and silver.

pf054.text: He took it all to a friend's in Bethnal Green.

pf055.text: That house was already full of others' goods.

pf056.text: Back home, he and his wife kept moving what was left.

pf057.text: Someone found him a barge for the goods. Whose things did he let aboard too?

pf058.text: Chests went over Tower Hill to the wharf.

pf059.text: Crowds jammed even the small gate.

pf060.text: A neighbor with a child put a few things on his barge.

pf061.text: Pepys hauled things too, not just giving orders.

pf062.text: That night the couple slept on bedding in his office.

pf063.text: No cookware: they ate leftovers from the day before.

pf064.text: Carts, boats, the garden: all used. What was still hard to move?

pf065.text: Early on September 4, goods still went to the boats; but wine in the yard stayed put.

pf066.text: By afternoon, the fire neared houses in Tower Street.

pf067.text: Neighbor Sir W. Batten, unable to move his wine, tried another way.

pf068.text: Batten dug a first pit in the yard for his wine.

pf069.text: Pepys seized the chance to put his office papers in it too.

pf070.text: That was just the first pit. And what of Pepys's own wine, as we asked?

pf071.text: At dusk he and Penn dug a second pit for their own wine.

pf072.text: They put their wine in, and he added that Parmesan from the start.

pf073.text: The entry that day gives no size or price for the cheese.

pf074.text: The cheese was hidden for now, but would the office escape the fire?

pf075.text: That night Penn sent for dockyard men to come at dawn and save the office.

pf076.text: Pepys wrote to Sir W. Coventry for leave to pull houses down.

pf077.text: But no answer came. Would someone in the street act first?

pf078.text: With wife and guests, he ate shoulder of mutton; no napkins.

pf079.text: Over supper he kept stepping into the garden to watch the sky burn.

pf080.text: At night he saw Tower Street houses in its path blown up.

pf081.text: Where houses were blown up, he noted, the fire stopped.

pf082.text: But could his own lane hold the next day?

pf083.text: Around 2 a.m. on September 5, his wife woke him again.

pf084.text: New cries of fire, by the church at his lane's end.

pf085.text: This time he at once took his wife and money downriver by boat.

pf086.text: Looking back by moonlight, London seemed almost all on fire. Would he go back?

pf087.text: He locked it at a friend's, telling wife and party to guard it in turns.

pf088.text: Then he went back by boat alone.

pf089.text: Passing Deptford on the way back, he saw his goods guarded on the barge.

pf090.text: He'd feared his house had burned, yet it stood.

pf091.text: The office was spared too; only up close was he sure.

pf092.text: The fire burned the dial and porch of the church at his lane's end, then stopped.

pf093.text: The diary credits blowing up houses and the workmen who rushed in.

pf094.text: He went to the church. What London would its tower show him?

pf095.text: From the church tower, he saw devastation all around.

pf096.text: Fire still raged afar; he didn't linger.

pf097.text: With embers scorching their feet, they walked on.

pf098.text: Moorfields was packed with refugees guarding their goods.

pf099.text: Pepys picked up a piece of glass warped by the heat.

pf100.text: That night he set workmen to watch the office.

pf101.text: Only at midnight did he lie down, and he slept better.

pf102.text: And by morning, was the fire in the City really out?

pf103.text: Morning, September 6: a new fire elsewhere in the City.

pf104.text: Pepys and the workmen rushed over and quickly put it out.

pf105.text: Houses and churches along the river were largely gone.

pf106.text: His goods were guarded on the barge, but not yet ashore.

pf107.text: At Deptford, he unloaded them at Sir George Carteret's.

pf108.text: Unloaded, he said nothing was missing or broken.

pf109.text: In his September 6 entry he wrote: our fears are behind us.

pf110.text: Was the cheese ever dug up? These entries don't say.

pf111.text: In that yard, what would you put in the second pit?
